April 1993 Interests The proliferation of faster
cheaper computers combined with wide spread network availability presents some interesting challenges
opportunities in the distributed computing area. For example

what system support is needed to simplify the development of scalable distributed applications or to deal with communication or device failures between parts of a distributed system? What needs to be done when a wireless device enters or leaves an area of coverage? What should devices do when they are in coverage areas that overlap. or how is a roaming device contacted? These are just some of the areas that I have been working on
following with great interest over the last while. In particular
much of my work has focused on designing
building system infrastructure to support the development
deployment of reliable

scalable distributed applications. promotion of novel
efficient
reliable methods in scientific computation
particularly for approximation
optimization problems involving differential equations with constraints. Thus
in addition to generally investigating properties of numerical methods I have been involved also in writing general-purpose mathematical software
investigating parallel algorithms
optimization techniques
solving inverse problems involving differential equations
getting more specifically involved in particular application areas such as multibody systems simulation
robotics
data inversion in geophysics
3D electromagnetic modeling
image reconstruction
cloth simulation
computational fluid dynamics. Awards Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada CAIMS

Faculty of Graduate Studies (1996-98). Research Groups Algorithms Lab Interests My research deals with topics in theoretical computer science. I am particularly interested in computational complexity

specifically the determination or characterization of the inherent computational difficulty of solving certain specific problems - or families of problems - on realistic models of computation. The problems that I am concerned with are fundamental combinatorial problems (including sorting
a number of basic graph theoretic problems
such as graph matchings
their generalizations)
geometric problems (including convex hulls
Voronoi diagrams
point location
geometric intersection
facility location
motion planning) that have widespread applications. While much of my research is based on a standard sequential deterministic model of computation
I am also interested in both parallel
distributed models of computation
the use of probabilistic algorithms. Awards CS-Can

pp. 392-403. Interests My PhD research areas were data mining
outlier detection. An outlier is an observation (point
tuple
record) in a dataset that doesn't seem to belong with the rest of the data. In other words
an outlier has sufficiently few points in its D-neighbourhood
for some given radius D. Data mining refers to the efficient discovery of previously unknown
potentially useful information from (large) datasets. Although most existing work in data mining has focused on the discovery of patterns or associations within data
one area that has been largely overlooked is the detection of outliers. Indeed
for some applications (e.g.
phone
credit card
or other financial transactions)
the patterns are well established
however
it is the exceptions to those patterns that are of interest. Our case studies include: NHL player performance statistics
stock market
mutual fund data
student performance in computer science courses. To account for scale
variability
correlation within the attributes (dimensions) of a multivariate dataset
to account for the adverse effects that some outliers may have on the search for outliers
we employ methods from robust statistics. Robust methods are said to accommodate outliers because they can handle many outliers before breaking down. For example
a single
very large outlier in a 1-D dataset can greatly inflate the mean
the standard deviation
at least 1
2 of the points would have to be sufficiently large in order to cause the median to reach undesirably high values. Thus
we say that the median is more robust than the mean. Most of my research was in CS education (evidence-based research
best practices in teaching
learning). While a Senior Instructor
I was also a part-time Science Teaching
Learning Fellow with UBC's Carl Wieman Science Education Initiative (2012-2014): http:
www.cwsei.ubc.ca. I have taught these courses multiple times at UBC: database systems
introductory programming
program design (C for engineering students
C++ for all)
operating systems
data structures
basic algorithms
discrete mathematics
scientific argumentation
peer review
technical writing
computer security
privacy

ethics. University of British Columbia(2001). Research Groups Artificial Intelligence Computer Vision Lab Research Centres CAIDA Interests I am interested in building working vision systems
both in robots
for using visual information for science
medicine
other applications. I am especially interested in early vision
especially computation of scene structure through stereo
motion
the integration of vision modules to produce robust systems. I am studying sensing
action for robots in dynamic environments
under a variety of operating constraints. The problems to be solved are not just system configuration
there are many open issues in determining the proper interactions between the vision component of a robot
the reasoning
action components. This requires investigating how world modeling requirements
computing system facilities can be combined into a vision-based operating system. These concepts are embodied in tracking systems
navigating mobile robots
other robotic systems. Two recent strong interests are seeing visual motion
adaptive triangulation for terrain representation. In the first
Jeff Boyd
I have built a system to recognize walking people using periodic variation in the 'shape of motion'
a description of the instantaneous distribution of motion in a moving figure. In the second
I use curvature descriptions of surfaces to isolate terrain features
which form the skeleton of a triangulated mesh approximating the terrain. This requires work in multiscale descriptions of surfaces
surface fitting methods
applications of computational geometry. Awards Semantic Robot Vision Challenge Precarn 20th Anniversary Commercialization Success Award Semantic Robot Vision Challenge Canadian Conference on Computer
Robot Vision Research Excellence

Canadian Inst. for Advanced Research. Research Groups Artificial Intelligence Research Centres CAIDA Interests The goal of my research program is to understand
build intelligent systems. I am particularly interested in the use of knowledge by agents who perceive
reason
act in the world. The central focus is constraint-based computational intelligence. The development of constraint programming
which we have pioneered
has already proven useful in a wide variety of applications in robotics
vision
scheduling
simulation
diagnosis
repair. Zhang
I have recently developed the online Constraint Net model for specifying
designing
verifying
simulating
implementing intelligent
embedded
real-time
hybrid systems
such as robots. In our Lab for Computational Intelligence (LCI)
we are building various sensor-based robotic systems. The overall framework is to characterize the knowledge that an intelligent system must have in its internal model
to show how it can acquire information about the world
integrate it into its model
then act to change the world. We are building teams of mobile robots
with real-time visually based control systems
for experimental tasks like soccer playing
navigation
telerobotics. We proposed

built the world's first soccer-playing robots. These systems provide a framework for driving the development of practical theories of real-time constraint-based computational intelligence. My main goal is to develop a clean theoretical
practical framework for the design

implementation of constraint-based agents. Canadian Inst. for Advanced Research (1992-95). Research Groups Artificial Intelligence Machine Learning Research Centres AMLTN CAIDA Interests My goal is to understand the principles behind action in natural
artificial agents. I consider the question: what should an agent do based in its preferences (or goals)
its background knowledge
(limited) perception of the environment
previous experience
limited computation? Currently
my main research interests consider theoretical
empirical investigations of automated reasoning built on the foundations of logic
probability
decision theory for tasks such as diagnosis
recognition
design
planning
reacting with partial knowledge
imperfect sensors. I ask what is a natural compact representation
how can aspects of it be exploited computationally. My main recent work has been in probabilistic reasoning
assumption-based logical reasoning. This includes developing a coherent theory
empirical studies based on building efficient implementations

developing methodologies for various applications. Different behaviour can be characterised by who chooses the assumptions: where nature chooses assumptions we have a logic-based characterisation of recognition
diagnosis incorporating probabilistic models such as Bayesian networks
much of the work on non-monotonic (default) reasoning can be seen as assumption-based reasoning where an adversary chooses the assumptions
where an agent can choose the assumptions we have a characterisation of design
planning. Combining these into a coherent framework that will look something like a logic-based decision
game theory with algorithms that exploit properties of various domains is a medium-term goal of my research. Other interests include: algorithms for probabilistic reasoning
diagnosis
decision theory
preference elicitation
robotics
user modeling
foundations of diagnosis
planning under uncertainty

University of British Columbia (2000-). Research Centres DFP Interests I would like to know how we see.
why we use the particular processes we do. Such knowledge would be useful in at least two ways: (i) it would help us design visual displays for optimal performance
(ii) it would help us design machine vision systems with the power
flexibility of natural vision systems. Plus
it would just be fun to know. Since I don't expect we'll find the answers to these questions any time soon

my concerns are focused on the slightly more restricted set of issues outlined above. My research over the past several years has involved mostly the first three of these issues. Much of this has centered around visual attention: what role it plays in humans
how to design interfaces so as to minimize attentional effort
the extent to which machines might need attention-like processes. As an example of such work

one of my projects at Cambridge Basic Research (CBR) explored the question of why people often do not see things that are right in front of their eyes. (This form of "blindness" is a major cause of traffic accidents.) To study why this happens
I developed a flicker paradigm in which two images - an original
a modified one - are sequentially alternated

with a brief (<100 ms) flash placed between the images. This flash is enough to drown out the local motion signals that would normally draw attention to the location of the change. Under these conditions subjects have a very difficult time seeing the change between the two pictures
even when the changes are large
the subjects are expecting them. Evidently
attention is required to see change
without it
people will look at but not see the change. (Take a look at some examples of this effect!) Awards 2011 CS Department Teaching Award 2009 CS Department Teaching Award Killam Research Prize

University of British Columbia (1997 - ). Interests I am interested in investigating ways in which Mathematical Logic
formal proof theory can be applied to various areas of Computing Science. I have been working on applications of set theory to programming language semantics
developing a language
called SetLog

which extends the traditional logic programming by providing (real) set abstractions. My goals are to study the applications of SetLog to databases. I am very interested in the techniques of Data Mining

more specifically in the discovery of temporal patterns. I am currently participating in a small group that is working on an efficient method for discovering sequential patterns that involve time constraints. I am also interested in software specification
verification. I am currently working on developing a logical language based also on set theory that will be useful for software requirements specification
analysis. The syntax of this formal language is very similar to Z
a notation that is successfully used for this purpose. The new theory would provide formal semantics for Z
the basis for formal analysis of Z specifications. Finally
I am interested in the use of multimedia technology in the design of courses or supplemental course material for university students. Ian Cavers
I are leading a project that investigates the use of Web-based technology for effective design
delivery of courses. Our lab is currently offering a series of interactive
self-paced

hyper-media courses that provide a comprehensive introduction to the computing resources available on campus. University of British Columbia (1997-). Research Groups Systems Research
construed broadly Interests The use of parallel computing is increasing with the growing demand for compute cycles
availability of high networks
inexpensive powerful commodity processors. As the use of parallel computing increases there is a growing need for system software that can deliver the hardware performance to the application
tools to help programmers design
construct
maintain parallel applications. The focus of my research is parallel computation on machines
systems where processes communicate by passing messages. I am interested in the use of message-passing libraries like MPI (Message Passing Interface)
PVM (Parallel Virtual Machine). Interests include the performance of libraries
tools to aid programmers in developing programs
design of message-passing applications to effectively use parallelism. Specific details about my research

current projects can be found in my homepage. University of British Columbia (1990-). Interests My goal is to make intelligent machines that see. Seeing is defined as the ability to interpret 2D images of a 3D world sufficiently well to carry out a specified task in the 3D world. Research consists of selecting a task
identifying the essential constraints of the task
defining computations that make vision possible for the task
implementing proof-of-concept computer systems to study performance in both real
experimental situations. My primary research contribution has been to demonstrate that radiometric constraints can be formulated
exploited in machine vision. Methods based on photometric stereo have been developed for determining dense representations of surface shape
including surface curvature. This work has application to the robot vision tasks of object recognition
localization

inspection. Current work extends to motion. Photometric stereo uses multiple light sources. Multiple light sources also support the determination of the optical flow created when objects (or a robot perceiver) are in motion. Current work has application to the tasks of deformable object measurement
robot navigation in dynamic environments. Another test-bed for my research is the computer interpretation of remotely sensed data. The practical goal is to extend the range of terrain

imaging conditions that can be handled by automatic image analysis systems. Recent work anticipates the routine availability of high spatial resolution (1m per pixel or better) satellite images for forest management
demonstrates the ability to recognize individual trees in such images. The availability
demand for remotely sensed imagery
other spatially-referenced data is increasing dramatically. The challenges for data retrieval
analysis
interpretation are substantial. I collaborate with researchers in databases
computational geometry

knowledge-based systems in the area of visual information management. Awards Faculty of Science Achievement Award for Service Submenu Leadership Former Leadership Faculty Staff In Memoriam Computer Science ICICS

faculty.title: Hutter, Domagoj Babic, Holger H. Hoos and Alan Hu - Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Formal Methods in Computer-Aided Design (FMCAD-07), pp. 27-34, 2007. SATzilla: Portfolio-based Algorithm Selection for SAT. Lin Xu, Frank Hutter, Holger H. Hoos, Kevin Leyton-Brown - Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Volume 32, pp. 565–606, 2008. Computational approaches for RNA energy parameter estimation. Mirela Andronescu, Anne Condon, Holger Hoos, David Mathews and Kevin Murphy - RNA 16(12): 2304-2318, 2010. Representing Score-Level Music Using the GUIDO Music-Notation Format. Holger H. Hoos, Keith A. Hamel, Kai Renz, and Jurgen Kilian - Computing in Musicology, Vol 12, MIT Press, 2001. Solving Combinatorial Auctions using Stochastic Local Search. Holger H. Hoos and Craig Boutilier - Proceedings of AAAI-2000, pp. 22-29, MIT Press, 2000. Interests Hard combinatorial problems occur in many areas of computer science and its applications, such as Artificial Intelligence, Bioinformatics, and Electronic Commerce. Although theoretical complexity results suggest that most of these problems are exponentially hard in the worst-case, this does not always mean that they cannot be solved reasonably effectively in practice. One of my primary research interests is to study hard combinatorial problems, and to explore algorithmic ways of solving them as efficiently as possible in practical applications. In this context, I am particularly interested in stochastic search algorithms that combine goal-directed, greedy search with randomised decisions. This group of algorithms includes general algorithmic techniques such as simulated annealing, evolutionary algorithms, ant-colony optimisation, or stochastic hill-climbing, as well as problem-specific algorithms. I have been working on various types of stochastic local search algorithms, investigated and modelled their behaviour, and developed new, improved algorithms for various applications, such as the satisfiability in propositional logic (SAT), the travelling salesperson problem (TSP), or winner-determination in combinatorial auctions. Currently, I am particularly interested in studying and developing stochastic search techniques for problems in bioinformatics, biocomputing, artificial intelligence, and electronic commerce. Although stochastic search algorithms are typically rather easy to implement, their behaviour is quite complex and presently not well understood. Much like other, more complex systems or algorithms, they are difficult to analyse theoretically. Therefore, empirical methodology is crucial for analysing and improving these algorithms. Compared to the methods used in other sciences, such as physics or biology, the empirical methodology for studying algorithms or systems in computer science is quite underdeveloped. I am working on improved methods for the empirical analysis of algorithms and use these methods for studying stochastic search algorithms. Such advanced empirical methods allow me to investigate and to model aspects of these algorithms' behaviour that are often not accessible to theoretical analysis. The potential of this approach is illustrated by recent breakthroughs in the development and application of algorithms for hard combinatorial problems that have been substantially facilitated by advanced empirical methodology. Computer Music is an exciting interdisciplinary field that combines artistic and scientific approaches and considerations; it has also strong links to fundamental issues in artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction. My work in Computer Music is focussed on software environments for the computer-assisted generation, manipulation, and analysis of score-level musical material as well as on the symbolic representations that provide the basis for such systems. or winner-determination in combinatorial auctions. Currently
I am particularly interested in studying
developing stochastic search techniques for problems in bioinformatics
electronic commerce. Although stochastic search algorithms are typically rather easy to implement
presently not well understood. Much like other
they are difficult to analyse theoretically. Therefore
empirical methodology is crucial for analysing
improving these algorithms. Compared to the methods used in other sciences
the empirical methodology for studying algorithms or systems in computer science is quite underdeveloped. I am working on improved methods for the empirical analysis of algorithms
use these methods for studying stochastic search algorithms. Such advanced empirical methods allow me to investigate
to model aspects of these algorithms' behaviour that are often not accessible to theoretical analysis. The potential of this approach is illustrated by recent breakthroughs in the development

application of algorithms for hard combinatorial problems that have been substantially facilitated by advanced empirical methodology. Computer Music is an exciting interdisciplinary field that combines artistic
it has also strong links to fundamental issues in artificial intelligence
human-computer interaction. My work in Computer Music is focussed on software environments for the computer-assisted generation

analysis of score-level musical material as well as on the symbolic representations that provide the basis for such systems.
